Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# ARC demonstration budget discipline

Use alongside general ARC grid reasoning when demonstrations are costly or capped.

## Workflow
1. After each pair, identify the exact proposition it establishes: color role, anchor, orientation, selection criterion, changed-cell rule, boundary behavior, or transformation class.
2. Compare the new pair with all previous pairs jointly. Separate genuinely new constraints from visual novelty; different colors or seed layouts may encode the same operation.
3. Keep a short list of live hypotheses and the specific evidence that distinguishes them. Request another pair only if its possible outcomes could separate those hypotheses and change the output.
4. Before a request, name the ambiguity it targets and account for remaining demo budget. Do not request merely because the rule still feels uncertain.
5. After several heterogeneous examples, pause to synthesize the shared operation and test it mechanically against all pairs. Check whether a general spatial rule explains them before fixating on an intuitive motif.
6. Once the evidence supports a rule, replay it cell-by-cell on every demo and apply it to the test. Near the cap, prefer the best-supported candidate over an uninformative request.

## Pitfalls
- Repeated requests without a discriminating question spend budget without improving inference.
- A different palette or seed appearance does not itself establish a different transformation.
- Uncertainty is not automatically actionable: another example helps only if it could alter the decision.
- A plausible verbal rule is not validation; derive exact changed cells and reproduce the outputs.

## Related guidance

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use for ARC-style visual/grid transformation tasks, including streams where tasks recur with fresh inputs.

## Recurring task-d2414d9a caution
This task ID recurred with demos using background colors 2/0 and marker 7, 6/0 and marker 9, 4/0 and marker 1, 6/0 and marker 2, 2/0 and marker 7, and 3/0 and marker 5. Outputs recolored large areas of background to the marker color. Flood-filling the marker-connected region using either 4- or 8-neighbor connectivity, and global recoloring, all failed on the test with background 6 and marker 5. No exact selection rule was established. Do not reuse a blanket flood-fill guess; infer precisely which cells are selected from the demos and replay it cell by cell.

## Recurring task-197199f9: extract center of 3x3 panels
A demo used an 18x18 input partitioned into 3x3 panels and produced a 6x6 output. The input consists of a noisy/background field (mostly 5, with 0s) plus solid 3x3 color blocks; output kept one center sample per panel in a 6x6 grid, mapping the background sample to 0 and preserving panel marker colors. Test 9x9 partitioned into 3x3 blocks solved as `[[6,2,7],[8,0,0],[8,0,0]]`: take each 3x3 region's center cell (row/col indices 1,4,7), and map center value 5 to 0; other colors remain. This suggests a center-downsample task with noise where center samples encode answer. Validate center-coordinate selection and color mapping against current demos before reuse.

## Recurring task-648a8222 unresolved completion task
A 29×24 test had background 5 and two separated irregular regions of color 7. Eight heterogeneous demos were requested and all eight test submissions failed. Examples differed in dimensions/palette and showed sparse edits to 1: a short 7-prefix extended to the right edge; an endpoint/small right-edge patch changed; selected repeated-looking pattern rows changed while similar controls remained untouched; a 27×26 example extended a partial 7-row from column 9 to the right boundary; a 10×10 example altered the last two cells of a 2-row; a 27×10 example altered the two rightmost cells of selected 8-rows; a 27×17 example changed a 4-column right-edge region in several rows. Some candidate outputs were unchanged despite similar repeated horizontal patterns. No reliable shared selection predicate was inferred. Failed test guesses included leaving the grid unchanged, recoloring alternating 7s in the upper area, and filling the lower region's right tail. Do not reuse these. Key unresolved question is why some row/region segments get recolored 1 while visually similar rows stay unchanged. Infer exact changed/unchanged coordinates from all demos and target a discriminating example; do not spend the entire demo budget without synthesis.

## Workflow
1. Parse dimensions, background, all non-background cells, and motifs; track coordinates consistently.
2. Request demonstrations when the rule is ambiguous. One plausible interpretation is not enough; use examples to distinguish local motifs, propagation, symmetry, and global rules.
3. Infer transformations from input-output differences. Identify changed cells and color mappings, then test candidate rules against every demo. Prefer a compact rule explaining all examples over intuition-based motif extension.
4. Apply the verified rule mechanically to the test. Preserve unchanged cells and dimensions unless evidence says otherwise; account for boundaries and overlaps.
5. Before submitting, reproduce every demo output exactly using the candidate rule. Check dimensions, row lengths, legal colors, and boundary behavior. If any demo fails, refine the hypothesis or request another demo.
6. Follow the protocol exactly: one valid action JSON per turn, on the final line. Submit only a complete grid; request a demo when further evidence is worth its cost.

## Pitfalls
- A salient multi-cell object in the test may be an instruction, seed, or unrelated element, not the rule itself. Establish its role from examples.
- Never generalize a local neighborhood mapping to every marker without checking the complete demo output. Wrong submissions consume attempts.
- Keep reasoning separate from the required response format; when the task requires one action, provide only that action.

## Validation checklist
- Candidate rule reproduces every demo exactly.
- Test output has intended dimensions and legal integer colors.
- Original non-background cells are preserved or changed only as specified.
- Boundary clipping and overlapping transformations are handled consistently.
- Final response contains exactly one action object.

# ARC hypothesis recovery and demo discipline

Use when a candidate has been rejected or demonstrations have not yet produced a validated rule.

## Workflow
1. Treat incorrect feedback as evidence against the entire submitted rule. Do not make a nearby speculative variant.
2. Re-extract demonstrations cell by cell: record changed coordinates, input-to-output color mappings, and salient cells that remained unchanged. Include boundaries and negative evidence.
3. Maintain a small set of explicit candidate rules. State what each predicts and what evidence would distinguish it.
4. Before requesting a demo, articulate the exact unresolved question and how possible answers would change the test output. If no plausible answer changes the decision, do not spend a request.
5. After a new pair, synthesize it jointly with all prior pairs before acting; do not issue serial requests without processing the latest example.
6. Validate a candidate mechanically against every demo, including unchanged cells and edges. Submit only when complete outputs match; otherwise request a targeted demo if budget permits.
7. In protocol-constrained ARC streams, output exactly one action object per response.

## Pitfalls
- “Extend the line” is not a verified transformation; specify affected cells, axes, colors, and endpoints.
- Visual novelty does not guarantee a demo resolves ambiguity.
- Repeating a guess with a small local change after rejection wastes budget and ignores evidence.

# ARC object-relation audit

Use this class-level checklist when a grid contains distinct objects in multiple colors, sparse singleton cells, or examples whose changed object is not obvious.

## Workflow
1. Segment non-background cells into objects/components; record each object's color, bounding box, shape, and singleton/line status.
2. Compare every demo input and output cellwise. Record changed cells and which object(s) changed; explicitly record conspicuously unchanged objects as negative evidence.
3. Test relational hypotheses before local shape-copy hypotheses: a marker may encode a target color or select an object by color, shape, adjacency, or position. Check whether the same relation predicts the changed object across demos with different palettes and layouts.
4. State competing hypotheses and the test prediction each implies. Request another demo only if a specific outcome discriminates them and could change the prediction.
5. Verify the complete predicted output, preserving all untouched cells and objects, before submission.

## Recurrence: task-561fb912 (8 demos, 8 failed submissions)
This stream presents varied grids with uniform backgrounds, multicolor objects and singleton/line markers. Exact observed demo edits (row/column 0-indexed):
- Pair 1: one isolated 2 at (2,11) -> 0; two 2 cells at (4,9),(5,9) -> 0. Other 2 and 3 shapes unchanged.
- Pair 2: 6 singleton (6,13) -> 4; 1 singletons at (7,12),(8,12),(9,11),(9,12),(10,10),(10,11),(10,12) remain 1; all other objects unchanged.
- Pair 3: 2x2 object at rows 3-4 cols 13-14 -> 9; singleton 2 at (5,14) -> 9. Rest unchanged.
- Pair 4: a 3x3-ish 9 component at rows 1-4 cols 12-14 selectively changed: (1,13),(1,14),(2,12),(2,13),(2,14),(3,14),(4,13),(4,14) -> 8; nearby 9 objects unchanged.
- Pair 5: 1 bar at row 8 cols 12-14 -> 8; other objects unchanged.
- Pair 6: 2 singleton (7,6) -> 1; other 2 features unchanged.
- Pair 7: 9 cells at (9,2),(9,3),(9,4) -> 3; other 9 remain.
- Pair 8: 3x3 4 object in upper right, rows 0-6 cols 7-9 (including its 3x3 shape) has its 3-colored cells at rows 0-2 cols7-8 changed to 4; 3 cells rows 0-2 col7 specifically; rest of object 4 unchanged. (Source pair exact edit: (0,7),(0,8),(1,7),(1,8),(2,7),(2,8): 3 ->4.)
Despite this ledger, no reliable shared selection rule was inferred and all 8 test submissions failed. Do not copy previous guesses or assume any of the mappings independently. Key durable lesson: different objects changed in each demo, with most lookalikes untouched; identify a relation across color/object roles and full-grid layout, and mechanically replay exact deltas before submitting.

## Pitfalls
- Do not infer a stamping operation just because a large shape and isolated markers coexist.
- Avoid serial demo requests without analyzing exact changes and updating hypotheses after each pair.
- A rule is not validated until it explains both changed and unchanged objects across every demo.
- In protocol-constrained ARC, send exactly one action JSON object per turn.
